items.title: Closing the import hole: no tsx, and an import policy
items.body:
Reference solutions live in `.ts` files. In v1 the worker inherited the server's `tsx` loader, so learner code could import those TypeScript files and read every answer. The fix has two parts. The worker now starts with `execArgv: []`, a bare Node with no `tsx`, so `.ts` curriculum files cannot be imported at all. On top of that, an import policy installed with `module.registerHooks` denies any `file:` URL outside the run directory and `node_modules`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **a separate OS user**: the journal does not do this; the fix is about what the worker can import, not file permissions.
- **move solutions into a database**: they stay in content files; they just become unimportable from the worker.
- **freeze harness globals**: that stops the `expect` forgery, a different attack; it does nothing about imports.

excerpts.quote: the worker inherited the server's `tsx` loader, so learner code could `import('../../content/index.ts')` and read every reference solution

`execArgv: []` — the worker is a bare Node, no `tsx` loader, so `.ts` curriculum files are unimportable. An import policy (via `module.registerHooks`) additionally denies `worker_threads`, `vm`, `child_process`, `module` and any `file:` URL outside the run directory and `node_modules`.

items.title: Why the agent asked before using a stored credential
items.body:
Using the stored token would have been fully automatic, but the journal gives two reasons it was the user's decision. **Visibility is irreversible in practice**: a public repo gets mirrored and indexed within hours, and only the user knows if they want it public. **Touching a stored secret is an escalation**: reading a credential out of the OS store and sending it to an API is something the owner should consciously approve. The token later turned out to have `repo`, `gist` and `workflow` scope, far more than a push needs.

Why the others are wrong:
- **the token had expired**: it worked; the author used it after approval.
- **the REST API breaks GitHub's terms**: creating repos through the API is normal; that was not the concern.
- **git push needs the gh CLI**: the entry says a plain `git push` would authenticate through the stored credential without `gh`.

excerpts.quote: **Visibility is irreversible in practice.** A public repo gets mirrored and indexed within hours.
**Touching a stored secret is an escalation.** Even on the user's own machine, reading a credential out of the OS store and sending it somewhere is an action they should consciously authorise.
That meant a plain `git push` to an *existing* repo would authenticate.

items.title: The signature of a load flake
items.body:
The author looked at the pattern of failures, not just the count. Three things together point to load, not a bug: every failure was the **same mode** (the worker's boot crossing the 60 s budget while importing jsdom and React DOM); the failing set **shrank from 6 to 3** between two full runs; and the first failing case **passed alone** in 31.8 s. A real code defect would usually fail the same way every time. A problem that comes and goes with how busy the machine is points to load.

Why the others are wrong:
- **same 6 failed identically on both runs**: they did not; the second run had 3 failures, which is part of the evidence.
- **only TypeScript lessons**: the failures were all react-environment cases.
- **typecheck failed first**: `npm run typecheck` was clean.

excerpts.quote: Every failing check is a react-environment case, every failure is the same mode — the worker's **boot** (importing jsdom + React DOM + the harness) exceeding the 60 s boot budget
the failing set shrank from 6 to 3 between the two full runs while the same case passed in 31.8 s run alone. That pattern says load flake, not code defect
`npm run typecheck` — clean (no diagnostics, exit 0).

items.title: The parent ignores the worker's ok
items.body:
After the fix, the parent never reads a verdict from the worker. It receives one row per test (`name`, `passed`, `error`) and works out `ok` itself: no run-level error, at least one row, and every row passed. You can see it in one line of `server/runner/index.ts`. So a worker that posts `ok: true` is simply ignored. To fake a pass, a learner would have to fake every individual row consistently, which the other fixes make hard.

Why the others are wrong:
- **rejects the run as forged**: the field is not treated as evidence of anything; it is just not read.
- **trusts it on the private port**: even rows on the private port do not carry a trusted `ok`; the parent always derives it.
- **cross-checks the worker's results.every**: the parent does its own `every` on the rows; it never asks the worker.

excerpts.quote: const ok = !error && tests.length > 0 && tests.every((t) => t.passed === true);
The parent never reads a verdict. It receives *rows* — one `{ name, passed, error }` per test — and derives `ok` itself: non-empty, every row passed, no run-level error.

items.title: What one isolated green run proves
items.body:
The case that failed in the full suite passed when run alone, in 31.8 s. The author is careful about what that shows: the grader's **logic** is fine for that case. It does not show that the **whole suite** would be green end to end on that machine; in fact, two full runs were not. "The logic works" and "the suite is green" are different claims, and the document refuses to swap one for the other.

Why the others are wrong:
- **raise BOOT_BUDGET_MS to 120 s**: the document does not draw that conclusion; it describes the gap rather than tuning it away.
- **the full suite is now green**: that is exactly the claim the author refuses to make.
- **single-case runs are never evidence**: the author does count it, as evidence about the logic.

excerpts.quote: The isolated green run is evidence the logic is fine; it is *not* evidence the suite would be green end to end here. Those are different claims, and this file refuses to trade one for the other.
ok   [react hook + event] ok=true 31788ms (boot 29867ms)

items.title: Start here: a journal, a sandbox, and an honest gap report
items.body:
This repo is a local learning app with its own built-in grader: learner code runs in a worker thread and the app scores it. The `upskilling/` folder is the mid-to-senior course built on top of the app, and nothing in it is executed. It is a journal of real decisions, verbatim code reviews, and a programme of missions.

This pack draws on three documents. Read them in this order:

1. `upskilling/README.md`: how the journal, reviews and roadmap fit together.
2. `upskilling/journal/002-shipping-with-a-stored-credential.md`: a short entry about pushing to GitHub with a credential nobody set up on purpose.
3. `upskilling/journal/005-where-the-trust-boundary-actually-is.md`: the grading sandbox could be fooled; this entry is the argument about what "fixed" should mean.
4. `upskilling/course/worked-examples/VERIFICATION-GAP.md`: why the worked-example folder holds a gap report instead of an example.

The journal entries follow one template (context, decision, alternatives, evidence, what I'd do differently). Read the "senior-level" section at the end of each one twice; most questions come from there.

excerpts.quote: Nothing here is executed by the app. It is a journal, a set of real reviews, and a programme.
**`journal/`** is where the learning actually lands. Entries follow one template — *context → decision → alternatives → evidence → what I'd do differently*

readMore.why: How the journal, reviews and roadmap fit together.
The programme of missions the journal entries come out of.

items.title: Posting on parentPort now reaches nobody
items.body:
The parent creates its own `MessageChannel` and hands one end, `port2`, to the worker in `workerData`. The worker copies that port into a module-scope constant and deletes it from `workerData` before any learner module loads, so learner code cannot find it. Results are only read from that private port. The ordinary `parentPort` is never read by the parent. So a learner who imports `parentPort` and posts fake rows is, in the journal's words, talking to nobody. (The import policy also denies `worker_threads`.)

Why the others are wrong:
- **a per-message signature**: there is no signing; the protection is which channel is listened to.
- **blocked only in TypeScript lessons**: the import policy is not described as lesson-specific.
- **postMessage throws**: posting on `parentPort` does not throw; it is simply ignored.

excerpts.quote: const { port1, port2 } = new MessageChannel(); const worker = new Worker(WORKER, { workerData: { ...data, dir, projectRoot, port: port2 },

The worker copies it into a module-scope constant and **deletes it from `workerData`** before any learner module loads. The ordinary `parentPort` is never read. Learner code that posts on `parentPort` is talking to nobody.

items.title: Concept: put the decision on the side you trust
items.body:
Whenever one component runs code written by someone else (a plugin, a webhook, a user script, a learner's solution), you have to decide **which side you trust**. Here the server (the parent process) starts a worker thread, and the worker runs the learner's code together with the test harness.

In v1, the worker computed the final verdict and sent it to the parent. Journal 005 lists three one-line "solutions" that produced a passing grade without solving anything, each by tampering with something inside the worker.

The entry's closing lesson is the general rule worth remembering. The instinct is to harden the untrusted side, but you can never be sure you closed every hole in code that someone else controls. The durable approach has two moves: the trusted side works things out for itself from evidence it can check, and the untrusted side is kept from reaching the trusted side's inputs. As you read the list of fixes in 005, sort each one into one of those two moves.

excerpts.quote: Learner code runs in a `worker_thread`. The worker hosts the test harness (`describe`, `it`, `expect`) as globals, imports the learner's module, imports the lesson's spec, runs the tests, and posts a result object to the parent.

The durable answer is to make the trusted side derive its conclusions from evidence it can check, and to make the untrusted side unable to *reach* the trusted side's inputs. Every fix listed above is one of those two moves.

readMore.why: The argument and the full list of fixes.

items.title: Captured builtins make prototype patches harmless to the core
items.body:
The trusted core of the harness uses a few builtins, `Array.prototype.every` among them. It copies them into local variables when its module is first evaluated, before any learner code exists. Learner code runs later. So if it replaces `Array.prototype.every`, the core keeps calling its saved copy and nothing it does changes. Only code **outside** the core, such as matcher bodies and pretty-printing, uses the ordinary methods; breaking those only breaks the learner's own run.

Why the others are wrong:
- **the verdict, via results.every**: that was the v1 attack; the worker no longer computes the verdict.
- **the run is aborted as a forgery**: nothing detects or aborts it; it just has no effect on the core.
- **Array.prototype is frozen**: the fix captures builtins into locals; it does not freeze `Array.prototype`.

excerpts.quote: is captured into locals at module evaluation, before learner code exists. A patched prototype afterwards changes nothing the core does. Everything *outside* the core (matcher bodies, pretty-printing) may use ordinary methods, because a learner who breaks those only breaks their own run.

items.title: Concept: claim only what you actually observed
items.body:
Both other documents in this pack share one habit: be exact about what your evidence shows.

- A command's output is not the same as its effect. A tool can print a cheerful success line while the result is not what you meant. Journal 002 shows how to check the effect directly before you call a job done.
- Order risky steps by how reversible they are. A local commit can be amended; publishing something cannot be undone. Do the safe local step first, and the outward-facing step after someone has agreed.
- A test run that did not go green is not something to round up. VERIFICATION-GAP.md was written because the author's baseline was not fully green that day. Instead of a worked example, it records exactly what ran, what failed, and what each run does and does not prove.

When a question asks "what does this run prove?", answer with the narrowest claim the output supports.

excerpts.quote: **The safe local step first, the outward-facing step after confirmation.** A commit can be amended; a public push cannot be unpublished.
the thing being demonstrated is that you do not publish a run you did not get.

readMore.why: The four senior-level points from the GitHub entry.

items.title: Verify the effect, not the command
items.body:
`git push` printing `main -> main` tells you the command ran. It does not prove the remote holds what you meant. The journal's check takes thirty seconds: compare the remote HEAD with the local HEAD, and list the files in the remote tree. That catches a specific class of bug: `.gitignore` silently excluded a file the project needs, so it was never committed or pushed, and every command still looked successful. In the entry the author confirmed the tree had exactly the 41 expected files.

Why the others are wrong:
- **push again with --force**: forcing rewrites remote history; it checks nothing and can destroy work.
- **git fsck locally**: that checks local object integrity; it cannot tell you a file was never committed.
- **check the README renders**: a nice look, but it would not notice a missing ignored file elsewhere.

excerpts.quote: **Verify the effect, not the command.** `git push` printing `main -> main` is not the same as "the remote has what I meant." Comparing SHAs and listing the remote tree is thirty seconds and catches the class of bug where `.gitignore` swallowed something load-bearing.
verified the remote HEAD equalled the local HEAD and that the tree on GitHub had exactly the 41 expected files and nothing gitignored.

items.title: The threat model of a local grader
items.body:
This app runs on the learner's own machine, for the learner. Nobody else's data is at stake. So the journal is explicit: the threat is not an attacker but **a learner fooling themselves**. If a one-liner can fake a pass, the app's record of progress stops being true, and that record is the whole point. The one genuine attacker case is someone on the same network using the grader to run code on the learner's machine, and binding to loopback plus checking the `Host` header closes that.

Why the others are wrong:
- **malicious npm packages**: not discussed as the threat; the hardening targets learner code inside the worker.
- **remote attackers stealing progress.json**: the server listens on loopback, so remote access is the case already closed separately.
- **other learners copying solutions**: it is a single-user local app; there are no other learners.

excerpts.quote: This is a *local* app. The threat model is not an attacker; it is a learner lying to themselves, and the value of the fix is that the app's claims about progress stay true. Binding to loopback and checking the `Host` header closes the one case where it is an attacker

items.title: Why the trust boundary is the parent
items.body:
The first reviewer's fixes (private channel, frozen globals, captured builtins) were all correct. The second reviewer asked a better question. The worker runs the learner's code, so the learner can change the worker's globals. If they control those, then **anything the worker computes is suspect**, even its report of whether the private channel was used honestly. Making the worker trustworthy against arbitrary code is a losing game. So the boundary is the parent, and the worker is treated as a source of untrusted data.

Why the others are wrong:
- **only the parent can import the spec under tsx**: the worker does import the spec; the argument is about trust, not loaders.
- **workers cannot send structured data**: they can; the worker sends rows over a `MessagePort`.
- **freezing is impossible under strict mode**: the fix does freeze harness globals; the point is that freezing alone is not enough to trust the worker.

excerpts.quote: If learner code controls the worker's globals, then anything the worker computes — including whether the private channel was used honestly — is suspect.
the worker must be made trustworthy, which is a losing game against arbitrary code), or the boundary is the **parent**, and the worker is treated as a source of untrusted data.

items.title: A slow grader boot leaves the attempt unscored
items.body:
When the worker takes longer than the 60 s boot budget, `abnormalEnd` returns the message "The grader took too long to start (this is not your code)" with `phase: 'boot'` and `timedOut: false`. The run has no test rows. `isScored` only counts a run that has rows, failed at compile or load, or timed out **after** becoming ready. None of those is true, so the run is **not scored** as an attempt. The learner loses nothing but time.

Why the others are wrong:
- **scored as a pass**: nothing turns a grader failure into a pass; `ok` is false.
- **retried automatically**: there is no background retry; the message tells the learner to try again.
- **scored as a failed attempt**: `isScored` returns false for this run, so it is not counted at all.

excerpts.quote: case 'boot-timeout': return { error: 'The grader took too long to start (this is not your code). Try again.', phase: 'boot', timedOut: false };
const isScored = (r: RunResult) => r.tests.length > 0 || r.phase === 'compile' || r.phase === 'load' || (r.timedOut === true && r.ready === true);
